    T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — September rainfall outlook, crop stress, sugar crushing season, inflation trajectory
    T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [YES] — winter crop planting risks, multi-season import dependency, RBI policy complications, rupee pressure

Synopsis:
    India's 2026 monsoon is tracking toward its weakest season in nearly two decades. A late June start, a 35% first-month deficit, a weak August, and a below-average September forecast are collectively stressing summer crops (cotton, soy, corn, rice, sugarcane) at critical growth stages. The ripple effects include reduced domestic supply across sugar, vegetable oils, pulses, and cotton — driving likely import increases from multiple origins. Food inflation (5.52% in July) is rising as the monsoon emerges as a fresh risk to India's CPI basket, which is more than one-third food. This complicates RBI policy: the bank had room to cut rates on the back of two years of above-average rainfall; a weaker monsoon could reverse that. The Iran conflict adds an additional commodity cost layer. The RBI now faces a stagflationary bind — weaker growth alongside stickier inflation — with potential negative spillover to foreign investment flows and the rupee.
